steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Bin picking
- object detection + motion planning + grasping; crucial for industrial automation
- trending research topic: challenges in image processing and path planning
- setup: 2D/3D camera (object/obstacle detection) + conveyor with bins
- vision detects object positions, obstacle shapes; motion planning computes path to grasp position
- efficient real-time path -> efficiency of mass production, assembly lines

2. Cycle
- machine vision + inverse kinematics + other algorithms -> best grasping configuration
- path planning: fixed home state -> grasp -> place state; then robot moves
- planning and movement serial, on the critical path -> planning + execution time drive cycle time and automation economics
- paths must be collision-free: obstacles + self-collision

3. Classical planners vs PPCNet
- classical planners usable but ignore repetitive nature of task
- static environment, robot cell runs for long periods: fixed initial configurations, fixed subspace of end-effector poses in bin
- PPCNet = Path Planning and Collision checking Network, deep neural network, for repetitive tasks
- generates waypoints, estimates collisions faster; safe, efficient path in short time
- beats conventional approaches on planning time; competitive path quality and success rate

4. Features
- end-to-end framework, easy to implement, efficient
- post-processing dataset generation improves path quality
- collision detection critical + time-intensive; PPCNet faster -> less planning time
- two training methods for collision checking network compared -> best and safest

5. Structure
- Sec 2 path planning techniques overview; Sec 3 problem definition; Sec 4 PPCNet + training; Sec 5 comparison with four state-of-the-art planners; Sec 6 conclusion

The vision system detects where the objects are and the shapes of the obstacles, and the motion planning module uses this information to calculate the path to the grasp position. Then the robot physically moves to complete the task. Since path planning and movement are serial and on the critical path, planning time and execution time are important factors for the overall cycle time and for the economics of the automation. It is also very important that the robot paths are collision-free, both with the obstacles in the environment and with the robot itself.

- classical planners usable but ignore repetitive nature of task
- static environment, robot cell runs for long periods: fixed initial configurations, fixed subspace of end-effector poses in bin

- beats conventional approaches on planning time; competitive path quality and success rate

- post-processing dataset generation improves path quality

- two training methods for collision checking network compared -> best and safest

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Bin-picking is an important part of automation in industry, and it includes object detection, motion planning, and grasping. In recent years bin picking has been a trending research topic because of the challenges it has in image processing and path planning. An industrial bin-picking setup has a 2D/3D camera that collects information about the environment (detecting objects and obstacles) and a conveyor with the bins. The vision system detects where the objects are and the shapes of the obstacles, and the motion planning module uses this information to calculate the path to the grasp position. If the manipulator has an efficient, real-time path, the efficiency of mass production and assembly lines can be improved a lot.

In a typical bin-picking cycle, machine vision, inverse kinematics and other algorithms are combined to find the best grasping configuration for the robot. When a configuration is found, path planning algorithms make a path from the fixed home state of the robot to the grasp, and then to a place state. Then the robot physically moves to complete the task. Since path planning and movement are serial and on the critical path, planning time and execution time are important factors for the overall cycle time and for the economics of the automation. It is also very important that the robot paths are collision-free, both with the obstacles in the environment and with the robot itself.

Classical planners can be used for bin-picking, but they often don't take advantage of the fact that the task is repetitive. In a static environment where a robot cell runs for long periods, path planning is limited to fixed initial configurations and to a fixed subspace of possible end-effector poses in a bin. In this paper we propose a path planner for bin-picking tasks that is more efficient in terms of planning time. We introduce the Path Planning and Collision checking Network (PPCNet), which is a tool based on a deep neural network and is designed for repetitive tasks like bin-picking. PPCNet generates waypoints along the path and estimates collisions faster, so it is a reliable solution for autonomous systems like robotic arms. With PPCNet we can generate a safe and efficient path in a relatively short time. Our method is better than conventional approaches in planning time and stays competitive in path quality and success rate, so it is a viable solution for industrial bin-picking applications.

The major features of this research are:

- 1. The PPCNet end-to-end framework we propose is easy to implement and is an efficient approach for path planning.

- 2. The post-processing dataset generation we propose improves the quality of the PPCNet paths.

- 3. Collision detection is a critical part of path planning and it takes a lot of time. PPCNet is faster, and because it can detect collisions quickly it reduces the planning time significantly.

- 4. We use and compare two different methods for training the collision checking network, to find the best and safest approach for collision detection.

The rest of the paper is like this. Section 2 gives an overview of various path planning techniques, with their advantages, disadvantages, and limitations for this problem. Section 3 gives the problem definition. Section 4 introduces our framework PPCNet and also discusses the training process. Section 5 evaluates our approach and compares its performance against four state-of-the-art path planners. Section 6 concludes the study.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Bin-picking, which includes object detection, motion planning, and grasping, is a crucial part of automation in industry. Bin picking has been a trending research topic in recent years because of the challenges in image processing and path planning [1,2]. Industrial bin-picking consists of a 2D/3D camera, used to collect environmental information (object and obstacle detection), and a conveyor with the bins. The vision system detects object positions and obstacle shapes, while the motion planning module calculates the path to the grasp position based on this information [3]. An efficient and real-time path for the manipulator can greatly improve the efficiency of mass production and assembly lines.

In a typical cycle of bin-picking operations, a combination of machine vision, inverse kinematics, and other algorithms is used to find the best grasping configuration for the robot. Once a configuration is found, path planning algorithms generate a path from the robot's fixed home state to the grasp, and then to a place state. Finally, the robot physically moves to complete the task. Because path planning and movement are serial and on the critical path, planning time and execution time are essential factors for the overall cycle time and automation economics. It is crucial to ensure that robot paths are collision-free, considering both obstacles in the environment and self-collision.

Classical planners can be used for bin-picking, but they often fail to take advantage of the repetitive nature of the task. In a static environment, where a robot cell operates for extended periods, path planning is limited to fixed initial configurations and a fixed subspace of possible end-effector poses within a bin. This paper proposes a path planner for bin-picking tasks that is more efficient in terms of planning time. We introduce the Path Planning and Collision checking Network (PPCNet), a deep neural network-based tool designed for repetitive tasks like bin-picking. PPCNet generates waypoints along the path and estimates collisions faster, which makes it a reliable solution for autonomous systems such as robotic arms. Using PPCNet, we can generate a safe and efficient path in a relatively short amount of time. Our proposed method outperforms conventional approaches in planning time and stays competitive in path quality and success rate, making it a viable solution for industrial bin-picking applications.

The major features of this research are as follows:

- 1. The proposed PPCNet end-to-end framework is an easy-to-implement and efficient approach for path planning.

- 2. The proposed post-processing dataset generation improves the quality of PPCNet paths.

- 3. Collision detection is a critical and time-intensive part of path planning. PPCNet offers a faster solution and significantly reduces planning time through its ability to detect collisions quickly.

- 4. We employ and compare two different methods for training the collision checking network to determine the best and safest approach to collision detection.

The paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we give an overview of various path planning techniques and discuss their advantages, disadvantages, and limitations for this problem. Section 3 outlines the problem definition. We then introduce our framework, PPCNet, in Section 4, where we also discuss the training process. In Section 5, we evaluate our approach and compare its performance against four state-of-the-art path planners. Finally, Section 6 concludes the study.

References:
[1] D. Buchholz, D. Kubus, I. Weidauer, A. Scholz, F. M. Wahl, Combining visual and inertial features for efficient grasping and bin-picking, in: 2014 IEEE international conference on robotics and automation (ICRA), IEEE, 2014, pp. 875–882.
[2] Y. Domae, H. Okuda, Y. Taguchi, K. Sumi, T. Hirai, Fast graspability evaluation on single depth maps for bin picking with general grippers, in: 2014 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA), IEEE, 2014, pp. 1997–2004.
[3] D. Buchholz, Bin-picking, Studies in Systems, Decision and Control 44 (2016) 3–12.
